symbols.meaning: integration variable of the original 1-D integral
auxiliary integration variable used to form the squared integral as a 2-D integral
substitution variable s = -r² used to evaluate the radial integral
value of the Gaussian integral, I = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{-x²} dx

steps.text: Write the square of the target integral as a product of two copies with independent dummy variables and combine into a single double integral over the plane: I² = (∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{-x²} dx)(∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{-y²} dy) = ∬_{ℝ²} e^{-(x²+y²)} dx dy.

Change variables to polar coordinates, x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, with area element dx dy = r dr dθ (the factor r is the Jacobian determinant of the transform), giving I² = ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^∞ e^{-r²} r dr dθ.
The θ-integral is trivial (the integrand is θ-independent), so I² = 2π ∫_0^∞ r e^{-r²} dr.
Substitute s = -r², so ds = -2r dr, i.e. r dr = -½ ds; as r runs 0→∞, s runs 0→-∞: 2π ∫_0^∞ r e^{-r²} dr = 2π ∫_0^{-∞} (-½) e^s ds = π ∫_{-∞}^0 e^s ds.
Evaluate the elementary integral: π ∫_{-∞}^0 e^s ds = π [e^s]_{-∞}^0 = π(e^0 - e^{-∞}) = π(1 - 0) = π. Hence I² = π.
Since e^{-x²} > 0 everywhere, I = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} e^{-x²} dx > 0, so take the positive square root: I = √π.

assumptions.assumption: The double integral ∬_{ℝ²} e^{-(x²+y²)} dx dy can be formed by multiplying the two 1-D integrals and evaluated by switching to polar coordinates (implicitly relies on the integral being well-behaved over the plane so the order of operations is valid).
assumptions.breaks_when: The source's own 'Complete proof' notes this needs justification via absolute convergence and Fubini's theorem when treated rigorously; that justification is a convergence argument and is out of scope here.

assumptions.assumption: The exponent is exactly -x² (coefficient 1, no shift), matching the polar substitution x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ used in step 2.
assumptions.breaks_when: For e^{-ax²} with a ≠ 1, or for e^{-x²+bx}, this exact sequence of steps does not directly apply without an added scaling or completing-the-square step not present in the supplied derivation.

failure_modes.mode: Sign error: using e^{+x²} instead of e^{-x²}
failure_modes.signature: The radial integral ∫_0^∞ r e^{r²} dr diverges, so I² has no finite value.
failure_modes.cause: Without the minus sign, e^{r²} grows without bound as r → ∞, so the substitution s = -r² no longer confines the s-range to a convergent exponential integral.

failure_modes.mode: Dropping the Jacobian factor r when converting to polar coordinates
failure_modes.signature: Computed value comes out as 2π ∫_0^∞ e^{-r²} dr, an integral with no elementary closed form, instead of π.
failure_modes.cause: The area element dx dy = r dr dθ is required by the coordinate change (step 2); omitting r changes what is being integrated and forfeits the elementary substitution in step 4.
